stem: Define the principal focus of a concave mirror.
solution:
**A number of rays parallel to the principal axis falling on a concave mirror are all reflected so that they meet at one point on the principal axis. That point is the principal focus of the concave mirror.**

It is represented by the letter **F**, and the distance from the pole to it is the **focal length**, \(f\).

This is what Activity 9.2 demonstrates with sunlight: the light from the Sun is converged by the mirror to a sharp, bright spot — the image of the Sun — and the heat concentrated there is enough to ignite a sheet of paper.

For a convex mirror the reflected rays do not meet; they only **appear to come from** a point behind the mirror, and that point is its principal focus.
groundedIn: §9.2 Spherical Mirrors with Fig. 9.2(a) and Activity 9.2, which define the principal focus as the point where rays parallel to the principal axis meet after reflection and give the burning-paper demonstration.

stem: The radius of curvature of a spherical mirror is 20 cm. What is its focal length?
solution:
For a spherical mirror of small aperture, the radius of curvature is **twice** the focal length:

\(R = 2f\), so \(f = \dfrac{R}{2}\)

\(f = \dfrac{20}{2} = 10\) cm

**The focal length is 10 cm.** This is the same as saying that the principal focus lies **midway between the pole and the centre of curvature**.
groundedIn: §9.2 Spherical Mirrors, which states that for spherical mirrors of small apertures the radius of curvature is equal to twice the focal length, \(R = 2f\), so the principal focus lies midway between the pole and the centre of curvature.

stem: Name a mirror that can give an erect and enlarged image of an object.
solution:
**A concave mirror**, with the object placed **between the pole and the principal focus**.

That is the one position of a concave mirror for which the image cannot be caught on a screen — it is **virtual, erect and enlarged**, and must be looked for in the mirror itself.

This is why concave mirrors are used as **shaving mirrors**, to see a larger image of the face, and by **dentists**, to see large images of a patient's teeth.

A convex mirror cannot do this: its image is always virtual, erect and **diminished**.
groundedIn: §9.2.1 Image Formation by Spherical Mirrors with Activity 9.3 and Table 9.1, which record the virtual, erect, enlarged image for an object between P and F, the uses-of-concave-mirrors passage, and Table 9.2 for the convex mirror always giving a diminished image.

stem: Why do we prefer a convex mirror as a rear-view mirror in vehicles?
solution:
For two reasons, and the second is the decisive one.

- **The image is always erect and diminished, whatever the distance.** A convex mirror never gives an inverted image, so the driver sees traffic the right way up, and the diminished image lets a large scene fit into a small mirror.
- **They have a wider field of view**, because they are **curved outwards**. This lets the driver **view a much larger area** behind the vehicle than a plane mirror of the same size would show.

A concave mirror would be useless here: its image can be inverted and real, depending on how far away the vehicle behind is.
groundedIn: §9.2.2, under Uses of convex mirrors, which states that convex mirrors are commonly used as rear-view mirrors because they always give an erect though diminished image and have a wider field of view, being curved outwards.

stem: Find the focal length of a convex mirror whose radius of curvature is 32 cm.
solution:
**Given.** \(R = +32\) cm (positive, since the centre of curvature of a convex mirror lies behind it).

\(f = \dfrac{R}{2} = \dfrac{+32}{2} = +16\) cm

**The focal length is 16 cm**, and the positive sign confirms that the principal focus lies **behind the mirror** — as it must for a convex mirror.
groundedIn: §9.2 Spherical Mirrors for \(R = 2f\), with §9.2.3 Sign Convention for Reflection by Spherical Mirrors, which makes distances measured behind the mirror positive.

stem: A concave mirror produces three times magnified (enlarged) real image of an object placed at 10 cm in front of it. Where is the image located?
solution:
**Given.** \(u = -10\) cm. The image is **real and three times enlarged**, and a real image in a mirror is **inverted**, so the magnification is **negative**:

\(m = -3\)

**Using the magnification formula.**

\(m = -\dfrac{v}{u}\), so \(v = -m\,u = -(-3)(-10) = -30\) cm

**The image is 30 cm from the mirror, on the same side as the object** — that is, 30 cm in front of it. The negative sign is what tells us so, and it is consistent with the image being real: a real image in a mirror is always formed in front of it, where a screen could catch it.

Taking \(m = +3\) here is the standard trap; an erect, enlarged image from a concave mirror would be **virtual**, not real.
groundedIn: §9.2.4 Mirror Formula and Magnification, which gives \(1/v + 1/u = 1/f\) and \(m = h'/h = -v/u\), with §9.2.3 Sign Convention for Reflection by Spherical Mirrors for the New Cartesian signs.

stem: A ray of light travelling in air enters obliquely into water. Does the light ray bend towards the normal or away from the normal? Why?
solution:
**It bends towards the normal.**

Water has a **higher refractive index** than air — \(n_w = 1.33\) against \(n_{air} = 1.0003\) — so water is the **optically denser** medium and air the optically rarer one.

The rule, and the reason behind it:

- **The speed of light is higher in a rarer medium than in a denser medium.**
- A ray travelling from a rarer medium to a denser medium therefore **slows down, and bends towards the normal**.
- Going the other way, from denser to rarer, it speeds up and bends **away from** the normal.

Here the ray goes from air (rarer) into water (denser), so it slows down and bends towards the normal.
groundedIn: §9.3.2 The Refractive Index with Table 9.3 and the optical-density note, which states that the medium with the larger refractive index is optically denser, that the speed of light is higher in a rarer medium, and that a ray travelling from rarer to denser slows down and bends towards the normal.

stem: Light enters from air to glass having refractive index 1.50. What is the speed of light in the glass? The speed of light in vacuum is 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
solution:
**The refractive index is the ratio of the speed of light in air to that in the medium:**

\(n_m = \dfrac{c}{v}\)

Rearranging for the speed in the medium:

\(v = \dfrac{c}{n_m} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^8}{1.50}\)

\(v = 2 \times 10^8\) m s\(^{-1}\)

**The speed of light in the glass is \(2 \times 10^8\) m s\(^{-1}\)** — two-thirds of its speed in vacuum, which is what a refractive index of 1.50 means.
groundedIn: §9.3.2 The Refractive Index, Eq. (9.7), which defines the refractive index of a medium as the speed of light in air divided by the speed of light in the medium.

stem: Find out, from Table 9.3, the medium having highest optical density. Also find the medium with lowest optical density.
solution:
Optical density is settled by the refractive index: **in comparing two media, the one with the larger refractive index is the optically denser**.

Scanning Table 9.3 for the extremes:

- **Highest optical density: diamond**, \(n = 2.42\) — the largest value in the table.
- **Lowest optical density: air**, \(n = 1.0003\) — the smallest value in the table.

Worth keeping separate from mass density: the book points out that an optically denser medium **may not** have the greater mass density — kerosene is optically denser than water although its mass density is lower.
groundedIn: §9.3.2 The Refractive Index with Table 9.3 and the optical-density note, which defines optical density by refractive index and warns that it is not the same as mass density.

stem: You are given kerosene, turpentine and water. In which of these does the light travel fastest? Use the information given in Table 9.3.
solution:
**In water.**

Since \(n = c/v\), the speed in a medium is \(v = c/n\) — so the **smaller the refractive index, the faster the light travels**.

From Table 9.3:

| Medium | Refractive index | Speed |
|---|---|---|
| **Water** | **1.33** | **fastest** |
| Kerosene | 1.44 | slower |
| Turpentine oil | 1.47 | slowest |

Water has the lowest refractive index of the three, so light travels fastest in it. This is the case the book flags: kerosene is **optically** denser than water even though its mass density is lower.
groundedIn: §9.3.2 The Refractive Index with Table 9.3 and Eq. (9.7), which gives \(n = c/v\) and the refractive indices of water, kerosene and turpentine oil.

stem: The refractive index of diamond is 2.42. What is the meaning of this statement?
solution:
It means that **the ratio of the speed of light in air to the speed of light in diamond is 2.42**:

\(n_{diamond} = \dfrac{\text{speed of light in air}}{\text{speed of light in diamond}} = 2.42\)

Two things follow.

- **Light travels 2.42 times more slowly in diamond than in air**, at about \(\dfrac{3 \times 10^8}{2.42} \approx 1.24 \times 10^8\) m s\(^{-1}\).
- Diamond has the **highest refractive index in Table 9.3**, so it is the **optically densest** medium listed — which is why a ray entering it bends most sharply towards the normal, and part of why cut diamonds sparkle.
groundedIn: §9.3.2 The Refractive Index with Eq. (9.7) and Table 9.3, which explains what a refractive index means using water at 1.33 and crown glass at 1.52 as worked readings.

subtopic: Lens Formula and Power of a Lens
stem: Define 1 dioptre of power of a lens.
solution:
**The power of a lens is the reciprocal of its focal length**, \(P = 1/f\), with \(f\) in **metres**. Its SI unit is the **dioptre**, written **D**.

**1 dioptre is the power of a lens whose focal length is 1 metre.**

So \(1\ \text{D} = 1\ \text{m}^{-1}\). A convex (converging) lens has a **positive** power, a concave (diverging) lens a **negative** one — which is why a prescription reads +1.5 D or –2.0 D.
groundedIn: §9.3.8 Power of a Lens, which defines power as the reciprocal of focal length, names the dioptre as the SI unit and fixes the sign for converging and diverging lenses.

subtopic: Lens Formula and Power of a Lens
stem: A convex lens forms a real and inverted image of a needle at a distance of 50 cm from it. Where is the needle placed in front of the convex lens if the image is equal to the size of the object? Also, find the power of the lens.
solution:
**Reading the signs off the description.** The image is **real**, so it is on the far side of the lens: \(v = +50\) cm. It is **inverted and equal in size**, so

\(m = \dfrac{h'}{h} = -1\)

**Object position.**

\(m = \dfrac{v}{u}\), so \(u = \dfrac{v}{m} = \dfrac{+50}{-1} = -50\) cm

**The needle is placed 50 cm in front of the lens.**

**Focal length.**

\(\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{50} - \dfrac{1}{-50} = \dfrac{2}{50} = \dfrac{1}{25}\)

\(f = +25\) cm \(= +0.25\) m

**Power.**

\(P = \dfrac{1}{f\ (\text{in m})} = \dfrac{1}{0.25} = +4\) D

The answer has a check built into it: an object at **\(2f\)** is exactly the position that gives a real, inverted image of the **same size** at \(2f\) on the other side, and \(2f = 50\) cm here.
groundedIn: §9.3.7 Lens Formula and Magnification, which gives \(1/v - 1/u = 1/f\) and \(m = h'/h = v/u\), with §9.3.6 Sign Convention for Spherical Lenses.

subtopic: Lens Formula and Power of a Lens
stem: Find the power of a concave lens of focal length 2 m.
solution:
**Given.** A **concave** lens, so by the sign convention its focal length is **negative**:

\(f = -2\) m

**Power.**

\(P = \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{-2} = -0.5\) D

**The power is –0.5 D.** The negative sign is not optional — it is what identifies the lens as **diverging**. Quoting “0.5 D” without it would describe a converging lens instead.
groundedIn: §9.3.8 Power of a Lens, which gives \(P = 1/f\) with \(f\) in metres and makes the power of a diverging lens negative, with §9.3.6 Sign Convention for Spherical Lenses.
